newsitem.title: UK: Thatcher reports deal UK Conservatives new blow.
newsitem.headline: Thatcher reports deal UK Conservatives new blow.

text.p: Intriguing reports that ex-prime minister Margaret Thatcher is impressed by opposition Labour leader Tony Blair have threatened to sour the ruling Conservative party's plans to mount a pre-election fightback.

Thatcher, ousted as prime minister in 1990 but still revered by many Conservatives, was said by the left-wing Tribune newspaper to have told the editor of The Times at a private gathering that if Blair won power, "he won't let Britain down".
Thatcher's office responded by saying it did not know where the report had come from and insisting she would be working hard during the coming campaign to get Prime Minister John Major re-elected.

"What she is on record as saying is that she thinks he (Blair) would make a disastrous prime minister," John Whittingdale, a Conservative who used to be Thatcher's parliamentary aide, told Channel Four television.
An endorsement of Blair by Thatcher would obviously be a harsh blow to Major's re-election hopes.
At the very least, the reports will reinforce the impression that the Conservatives are contemplating defeat after 18 unbroken years in power.
An opinion poll in Friday's Independent newspaper showed Labour had maintained its large lead over the Conservatives and were 25 points ahead.

The Harris poll showed support for Labour had dropped one point to 52 percent from its most recent poll, carried out last week. The Conservatives dropped three points to 27 percent while the minority Liberal Democrats rose four points to 14 percent.

Labour gleefully circulated a memo from the ruling party's communications director asking its legislators not to cooperate with three usually pro-Conservative papers he said were trying to work up "unhelpful stories about the state of party morale".
Major on Thursday kept Britain guessing about the date of the election by telling a regional newspaper that there would be no announcement this week.
Speculation immediately switched to a statement next week, which would in effect fire the starting gun for a six-week campaign if, as expected, Major plumps for an election on May 1.
Conservative chairman Brian Mawhinney is likely to fuel the speculation of an early announcement when he addresses the party's spring conference on Friday in the western city of Bath.
"We're going to have the strongest, longest and hardest-fought Conservative election campaign in our history," Mawhinney is expected to tell activists, according to an aide.
A number of Conservative strategists want Major to end the waiting game because they sense Labour could crack under the strain of a protracted campaign.
Major addresses the conference on Saturday and is expected to unveil proposals for leading sportsmen to fan out as ambassadors through British schools to promote sport.
The project, close to Major's heart, would be funded by the proceeds of Britain's national lottery, aides said.
